content: Children who consumed fortified complementary foods demonstrated significantly better mental skill development and overall psychomotor development scores compared to those consuming unfortified complementary foods. However, no significant differences were observed when fine and gross motor scores were assessed separately. This review analyzed findings from 16 studies published between 1977 and 2020. Most studies were conducted in lowor middle-income countries, often in malaria-endemic regions. The fortified foods and micronutrients used for fortification varied widely, with most studies focusing on iron, either alone or in combination with other micronutrients. The fortified foods primarily included cereal-based products (e.g., wheat, maize, rice, and millet), with only two studies using cereal-legume blends and one study using fortified legumes. Five studies targeted children aged 6–11 months, seven studies included children aged 12–23 months, and one study included children aged 6–23 months. Three studies had a broader age range, including children aged 6–60 months. The findings of this review are applicable to apparently healthy, non-hospitalized children in lowand middle-income countries in Asia and Africa, although some children in these settings may be at risk of diseases such as malaria, diarrhea, or malnutrition. While complementary food fortification may also have implications for children in high-income countries, there is a lack of studies investigating its effects in these populations. The use of fortified complementary foods in the reviewed studies was primarily for preventive purposes, and the review does not evaluate their effectiveness in treating malnutrition. Outcomes such as length-for-age z-scores, ferritin concentrations, body iron, serum zinc, fine motor scores, and gross motor scores were judged to have low certainty. Outcomes like free erythrocyte porphyrin, diarrhea, acute respiratory tract diseases, and fever were judged to have very low certainty. Evidence was downgraded due to design limitations (risk of bias), inconsistency, and imprecision. The review process aimed to minimize bias by employing a broad search strategy across electronic databases and trial registries without language restrictions. While it is unlikely that published trials were missed, unpublished or ongoing trials not registered in clinical trial registries may have been overlooked. At least two review authors independently conducted trial selection, data extraction, and risk of bias and GRADE assessments. Funnel plots were used to explore publication bias for hemoglobin concentration, but other outcomes were investigated in fewer than 10 trials, limiting this analysis. This is the first systematic review summarizing evidence on the consumption of fortified complementary foods compared to unfortified versions in children aged 6–23 months. Previous reviews have assessed the health effects of centrally processed micronutrient-fortified foods in children aged 6 months to 5 years and 5 to 15 years, including fortified dairy and cereal products. However, this review excluded milk formula and fortified milk-based products. Other reviews have concluded that food fortification with micronutrients is effective in reducing anemia during the complementary feeding period in developing countries, but evidence for functional health outcomes remains sparse. These conclusions align with the findings of this review. Conclusions and Implications for Practice The use of centrally fortified complementary foods is likely an effective intervention to reduce anemia in infants and young children aged 6 months to 2 years in malaria-endemic regions. This intervention can be integrated into strategies to prevent anemia in this age group. Evidence from two studies suggests that consuming fortified complementary foods may slightly improve mental and motor development scores. However, the effects of fortification on growth outcomes appear minimal, and there is no significant difference in the acceptability of fortified versus unfortified foods among children aged 6–23 months. Current evidence does not show improvements in zinc and vitamin A status, and there is no data on other vitamins and minerals. Implications for Research Further research is needed to explore whether fortified complementary foods: 1. Impact all-cause mortality. 2. Have any adverse effects. 3. Lead to adequate or excessive nutrient intakes (and at what level of fortification). 4. Affect stunting or wasting. 5. Influence vitamin and mineral status beyond iron. 6. Improve mental and motor skill development under specific circumstances. 7. Alter gut microbiota composition. 8. Affect taste preferences. 9. Displace other foods in the diet. Studies with varying nutrient content should be conducted to determine dose-response effects. The effects of complementary food fortification should be further investigated in both developing and high-income countries, as well as in non-malaria-endemic regions. Future randomized controlled trials should employ rigorous methodologies and include large sample sizes.
